question: Who makes the benchmarks, and do their scores carry clear meaning?

summary.independence_rule: independent is false when any frontier lab, or any data vendor selling to labs, created, co-authored or funded the benchmark.

findings.claim: Leading models lost up to 8% accuracy on GSM1k, a fresh set of grade school problems written to mirror GSM8K, and several model families showed systematic overfitting.
findings.source_title: A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic
findings.quote: When evaluating leading open- and closed-source LLMs on GSM1k, we observe accuracy drops of up to 8%, with several families of models showing evidence of systematic overfitting across almost all model sizes.

findings.claim: Asked to fill in one masked wrong answer option on MMLU, ChatGPT and GPT-4 reproduced it exactly 52% and 57% of the time. That points to test data seen in training.
findings.source_title: Investigating Data Contamination in Modern Benchmarks for Large Language Models
findings.quote: Further, in the MMLU benchmark, ChatGPT and GPT-4 demonstrated an exact match rate of 52\% and 57\%, respectively, in guessing the missing options in benchmark test data.

findings.claim: Contamination testing confirmed by human review found GPT-4 had seen test or validation splits of AG News, WNLI (a GLUE task) and XSum during pretraining.
findings.source_title: Time Travel in LLMs: Tracing Data Contamination in Large Language Models
findings.quote: The human evaluation reveals that the train and test/validation splits of both the AG News and WNLI datasets were included in GPT-4’s pre-training data. However, for IMDB and RTE, only the training partitions were incorporated, while for XSum, only the test split was leaked.

findings.claim: A study of 31 language models found substantial evidence of training on test sets for math benchmarks such as GSM8K and MATH, which makes score comparisons unfair.
findings.source_title: Benchmarking Benchmark Leakage in Large Language Models
findings.quote: By analyzing 31 LLMs under the context of mathematical reasoning, we reveal substantial instances of training even test set misuse, resulting in potentially unfair comparisons.

findings.claim: HumanEval overlaps with public pretraining data by 12.2% (Pile) to 18.9% (Stack). StarCoderBase scored 75% on HumanEval problems most similar to its training data and 31.3% on those least similar.
findings.source_title: Quantifying Contamination in Evaluating Code Generation Capabilities of Language Models
findings.quote: StarCoderBase-15.5B achieves an accuracy of 72% on the top 10% of questions and an accuracy of 22% on the bottom 10% of questions of the MBPP benchmark.

findings.claim: In SWE-bench, 32.67% of patches judged successful had their solution leaked in the issue text and 31.08% passed only because tests were weak.
findings.source_title: SWE-Bench+: Enhanced Coding Benchmark for LLMs
findings.quote: 2) 31.08% of the passed patches are suspicious patches due to weak test cases, i.e., the tests were not adequate to verify the correctness of a patch.

findings.claim: Models named the buggy file from issue text alone with up to 76% accuracy on SWE-bench repositories but up to 53% on outside repositories, pointing to memorization.
findings.source_title: The SWE-Bench Illusion: When State-of-the-Art LLMs Remember Instead of Reason
findings.quote: We show that state-of-the-art models achieve up to 76% accuracy in identifying buggy file paths using only issue descriptions, without access to repository structure.

findings.claim: DeepSeek-Base-33B solved about 60% of LeetCode problems from May 2023 on first try (Pass@1) and about 0% from September 2023, after its training cutoff.
findings.source_title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
findings.quote: Interestingly, we find that even the DS-Base-33B model also suffers from contamination dropping from Pass@1 ∼60 in May problems to Pass@1 ∼0 in September LeetCode problems.

findings.claim: Pass rates on Codeforces and Project Euler problems tracked GitHub popularity and release dates before training cutoffs, which the authors call strong evidence of contamination.
findings.source_title: Data Contamination Through the Lens of Time
findings.quote: Specifically, we consider two code/mathematical problem-solving datasets, Codeforces and Project Euler, and find statistically significant trends among LLM pass rate vs. GitHub popularity and release date that provide strong evidence of contamination.

findings.claim: On functional variants of MATH that change numbers but keep reasoning, top models showed a reasoning gap of 58.35% to 80.31% against their static-set scores.
findings.source_title: Functional Benchmarks for Robust Evaluation of Reasoning Performance, and the Reasoning Gap
findings.quote: We find reasoning gaps from 58.35% to 80.31% among the state-of-the-art closed and open weights models that perform well on static benchmarks, with the caveat that the gaps are likely to be smaller with more sophisticated prompting strategies.

findings.claim: OpenAI stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified in 2026 after finding every frontier model it tested could reproduce gold patches or problem specifics, meaning all had seen some tasks in training.
findings.source_title: Why SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding capabilities
findings.quote: In our analysis we found that all frontier models we tested were able to reproduce the original, human-written bug fix used as the ground-truth reference, known as the gold patch, or verbatim problem statement specifics for certain tasks, indicating that all of them have seen at least some of the problems and solutions during training.

findings.claim: Classifiers lost 11% to 14% accuracy on a new ImageNet test set built with ImageNet's original procedure, so part of measured progress did not carry over to fresh data.
findings.source_title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
findings.quote: We evaluate a broad range of models and find accuracy drops of 3% - 15% on CIFAR-10 and 11% - 14% on ImageNet.

findings.claim: At least 6% of ImageNet's validation set is mislabeled, enough to change which models rank highest.
findings.source_title: Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks
findings.quote: Errors in test sets are numerous and widespread: we estimate an average of at least 3.3% errors across the 10 datasets, where for example label errors comprise at least 6% of the ImageNet validation set.

findings.claim: Manual review found errors in 57% of questions in MMLU's virology subset.
findings.source_title: Are We Done with MMLU?
findings.quote: For example, we find that 57% of the analysed questions in the Virology subset contain errors.

findings.claim: FutureHouse estimated about 29% of the text-only chemistry and biology answers in Humanity's Last Exam are contradicted by peer-reviewed literature.
findings.source_title: About 30% of Humanity’s Last Exam Chemistry/biology Answers are Likely Wrong
findings.quote: We found that 29 ± 3.7% (95% CI) of the text-only chemistry and biology questions had answers with directly conflicting evidence in peer reviewed literature.

findings.claim: Meta privately tested 27 model variants on Chatbot Arena before releasing Llama 4, and the study shows such selective disclosure inflates arena rankings.
findings.source_title: The Leaderboard Illusion
findings.quote: At an extreme, we identify 27 private LLM variants tested by Meta in the lead-up to the Llama-4 release.

findings.claim: Llama 4 Maverick ranked second on LMArena via an experimental chat version, which differed from Meta's release to developers.
findings.source_title: Meta's benchmarks for its new AI models are a bit misleading
findings.quote: But it seems the version of Maverick that Meta deployed to LM Arena differs from the version that’s widely available to developers.

findings.claim: METR found frontier models gaming their scoring in evaluation tasks, with reward hacking more than 43 times as common on RE-Bench tasks as on HCAST tasks.
findings.source_title: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
findings.quote: Reward hacking was more than 43× more common on RE-Bench tasks than HCAST tasks, perhaps because on RE-Bench tasks the model was able to see the entire scoring function, making that function easier to bypass and inadvertently priming the model to consider that type of solution more strongly.

findings.claim: OpenAI's o3 system, which scored 75.7% on ARC-AGI-1 under its $10,000 compute limit, had been trained on that benchmark's public training set.
findings.source_title: OpenAI o3 Breakthrough High Score on ARC-AGI-Pub
findings.quote: OpenAI's new o3 system - trained on the ARC-AGI-1 Public Training set - has scored a breakthrough **75.7%** on the Semi-Private Evaluation set at our stated public leaderboard $10k compute limit.

findings.claim: OpenAI commissioned 300 FrontierMath problems from Epoch AI and owns their statements and solutions, apart from a 50-question holdout set.
findings.source_title: Clarifying the creation and use of the FrontierMath benchmark
findings.quote: OpenAI commissioned Epoch AI to produce 300 advanced math problems for AI evaluation that form the core of the FrontierMath benchmark.

findings.claim: Humanity's Last Exam, made by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI, launched with 2,500 questions on which frontier models showed low accuracy and poor calibration.
findings.source_title: Humanity's Last Exam
findings.quote: State-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate low accuracy and calibration on HLE, highlighting a significant gap between current LLM capabilities and the expert human frontier on closed-ended academic questions.

findings.claim: APEX-Agents, built by the hiring firm Mercor, launched with frontier models completing fewer than 25% of tasks taking professionals hours.
findings.source_title: Introducing APEX-Agents
findings.quote: Frontier models successfully complete less than 25% of tasks that would typically take professionals hours.

findings.claim: Dynabench's authors chart time to estimated human performance shrinking from decades for MNIST to a few years for newer datasets, with GLUE passed within one year of release.
findings.source_title: Dynabench: Rethinking Benchmarking in NLP
findings.quote: While it used to take decades for machine learning models to surpass estimates of human performance on benchmark tasks, that milestone is now routinely reached within just a few years for newer datasets (see Figure 1).

findings.claim: GLUE was saturated within one year of its release, and SuperGLUE in less time.
findings.source_title: Plotting Progress in AI
findings.quote: When GLUE was introduced, it was saturated within a year.

findings.claim: Across 1,079 benchmark metric trajectories, 378 (about 35%) showed saturation or stagnation.
findings.source_title: Mapping the global dynamics of AI benchmark creation, utilization, and saturation
findings.quote: Cluster 2 (378 benchmarks), corresponds to the saturation/stagnation scenario.

findings.claim: Within a year of their introduction, scores rose 18.8 points on MMMU and 48.9 points on GPQA, and SWE-bench went from 4.4% to 71.7% solved.
findings.source_title: The 2025 AI Index Report | Stanford HAI
findings.quote: By 2024, AI performance on these benchmarks saw remarkable improvements, with gains of 18.8 and 48.9 percentage points on MMMU and GPQA, respectively.

findings.claim: Raji and co-authors argue benchmarks such as ImageNet and GLUE are presented as measures of general capability that no fixed dataset can provide.
findings.source_title: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark
findings.quote: In this position paper, we explore the limits of such benchmarks in order to reveal the construct validity issues in their framing as the functionally "general" broad measures of progress they are set up to be.

findings.claim: Bowman and Dahl set four criteria for language understanding benchmarks and argue most current ones fail them.
findings.source_title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?
findings.quote: In this position paper, we lay out four criteria that we argue NLU benchmarks should meet.

findings.claim: One review of 445 language model benchmarks found recurring design patterns that undermine claims drawn from them.
findings.source_title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
findings.quote: Across the reviewed articles, we find patterns related to the measured phenomena, tasks, and scoring metrics which undermine the validity of the resulting claims.

findings.claim: One assessment of 24 AI benchmarks found most do not report statistical significance of their results.
findings.source_title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices
findings.quote: We further find that most benchmarks do not report statistical significance of their results nor allow for their results to be easily replicated.

findings.claim: In interviews with 19 practitioners, benchmarks helped compare models but were often inadequate for product and policy decisions.
findings.source_title: More than Marketing? On the Information Value of AI Benchmarks for Practitioners
findings.quote: Based on the analyses of interviews with 19 individuals who have used, or decided against using, benchmarks in their day-to-day work, we find that across these settings, participants use benchmarks as a signal of relative performance difference between models.

findings.claim: Software tasks frontier models can complete half the time have doubled in length about every seven months since 2019.
findings.source_title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
findings.quote: Furthermore, frontier AI time horizon has been doubling approximately every seven months since 2019, though the trend may have accelerated in 2024.

findings.claim: In one randomized trial, experienced open-source developers took 19% longer to finish issues with AI tools, after expecting a 24% speedup.
findings.source_title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
findings.quote: When developers are allowed to use AI tools, they take 19% longer to complete issues, a significant slowdown that goes against developer beliefs and expert forecasts.

findings.claim: None of the four agent pull requests that passed human-written tests were mergeable as-is when METR reviewed them by hand.
findings.source_title: Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation
findings.quote: However, when manually reviewing a subset of these PRs^6^, none of them are mergeable as-is.

findings.claim: On GDPval tasks, Claude Opus 4.1 was rated as good as or better than human experts on just under half.
findings.source_title: Measuring the performance of our models on real-world tasks
findings.quote: Claude Opus 4.1 produced outputs rated as good as or better than humans in just under half the tasks.

findings.claim: Remote Labor Index's best AI agent automated 2.5% of its paid freelance projects.
findings.source_title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work
findings.quote: AI agents perform near the floor on RLI, with the highest-performing agent achieving an automation rate of 2.5%.

findings.claim: When OSWorld launched, humans completed 72.36% of its computer tasks and its best model 12.24%.
findings.source_title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
findings.quote: While humans can accomplish over 72.36% of the tasks, the best model achieves only 12.24% success, primarily struggling with GUI grounding and operational knowledge.

findings.claim: An MIT report found about 95% of enterprise generative AI pilots produced no measurable effect on profit and loss.
findings.source_title: MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing
findings.quote: Despite the rush to integrate powerful new models, about 5% of AI pilot programs achieve rapid revenue acceleration; the vast majority stall, delivering little to no measurable impact on P&L.

findings.claim: Prices to reach fixed benchmark scores fell between 9 and 900 times per year depending on task.
findings.source_title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks
findings.quote: The rate of decline varies dramatically depending on the performance milestone, ranging from 9x to 900x per year.

findings.claim: 78% of organizations reported using AI in 2024, but most that reported cost savings put them below 10%.
findings.source_title: The 2025 AI Index Report
findings.quote: 49% of respondents whose organizations use AI in service operations report cost savings, followed by supply chain management (43%) and software engineering (41%), but most of them report cost savings of less than 10%.

glue.note: A DeepMind researcher is a co-author.

superglue.org: NYU, Facebook AI, University of Washington, DeepMind

mmlu.org: UC Berkeley and others (Dan Hendrycks et al.)

math-level-5.note: Epoch AI runs the evaluations reported here.

swe-bench-verified.type: frontier lab subset of an academic benchmark
swe-bench-verified.note: OpenAI later stopped reporting it, citing contamination.

arc-agi-1.note: Chollet worked at Google when he released it.

humanitys-last-exam.org: Center for AI Safety and Scale AI
humanitys-last-exam.note: Scale AI sells training data to AI labs.

frontiermath.note: OpenAI owns most problems and solutions.

osworld.org: XLANG Lab, University of Hong Kong, with Salesforce, CMU, Waterloo

osworld-2.org: XLANG Lab, University of Hong Kong

apex-agents.note: Mercor supplies expert data to AI labs.
